text:
“Oh, Mama, how can you say such a thing? Of course, when our dear relations drive up in winter and stay for six hours, or perhaps even longer, and Aunt Gundel and Aunt Olga scrutinize me and find me pert—and Aunt Gundel once told me so, too—yes, then things are sometimes not very pleasant, I must admit. But otherwise I have always been happy here, so happy.”

And as she said this, she flung herself, weeping violently, onto her knees before Mama and kissed both her hands.

“Get up, Effi. Those are moods that come over one when one is as young as you are and is facing marriage and the unknown. But now read me the letter, unless it contains something quite exceptional, or perhaps secrets.”

“Secrets,” Effi laughed, and sprang up again, her mood suddenly transformed. “Secrets! Yes, he is always making a start at them, but most of it I could have posted at the mayor’s office, where the district administrator’s ordinances are always displayed. Well, Geert is a district administrator, after all.”

“Read, read.”

“Dear Effi! ... That is how it always begins, you see, and sometimes he also calls me his ‘little Eve.’”

“Read, read ... You are supposed to be reading.”

“Very well: Dear Effi! The nearer we come to our wedding day, the more sparing your letters become. When the post arrives, I always look first for your handwriting, but, as you know (and indeed I did not wish it otherwise), usually in vain. The workmen are now in the house, preparing the rooms—only a few of them, to be sure—for your arrival. The best of it will probably not be done until we are away on our journey. Madelung, the upholsterer, who supplies everything, is a character, and I shall tell you about him next time, but above all about how happy I am because of you, because of my sweet little Effi. The ground here is burning beneath my feet, and meanwhile our good town is growing ever quieter and lonelier. The last bathing visitor left yesterday; toward the end he bathed in nine-degree water, and the bathing attendants were always glad when he emerged unscathed. For they feared he might have a stroke, which would then bring the resort into disrepute, as though the waves here were worse than elsewhere. I rejoice when I think that in only four weeks I shall be sailing with you from the Piazzetta to the Lido, or over to Murano, where they make glass beads and beautiful jewelry. And may the most beautiful be for you. Many greetings to your parents, and the tenderest kiss to you from your Geert.” Effi folded the letter again to put it into the envelope.

“That is a very nice letter,” said Frau von Briest, “and the fact that he maintains the proper measure in everything is one merit more.”

“Yes, the proper measure—he maintains that.”

“My dear Effi, let me ask you a question: would you wish that the letter did not maintain the proper measure; would you wish it were more tender, perhaps effusively tender?”

“No, no, Mama. Truly and honestly, no; I do not wish that. It is better this way, after all.”

“It is better this way, after all. Just listen to how that sounds. You are so peculiar. And then you were crying earlier. Is there something weighing on your heart? There is still time. Do you not love Geert?”

“Why should I not love him? I love Hulda, and I love Bertha, and I love Hertha. And I love old Niemeyer too. And that I love you both goes without saying. I love everyone who means well by me and is kind to me and spoils me. And Geert will probably spoil me too. In his own way, of course. He already intends to give me jewelry in Venice. He has no idea that I care nothing for jewelry. I would rather climb, and I would rather swing, and best of all always with the fear that something somewhere might tear or break and that I might fall. It will hardly cost me my head straightaway.”

“And perhaps you also love your cousin Briest?”

“Yes, very much. He always cheers me up.”

“And would you have liked to marry Cousin Briest?”

“Marry him? For heaven’s sake, no. He is still half a boy. Geert is a man, a handsome man, a man with whom I can make an impression and who will amount to something in the world. Whatever are you thinking, Mama?”

“Well, that is good, Effi; that pleases me. But there is still something on your mind.”

“Perhaps.”

“Well, speak.”

“Look, Mama, that he is older than I am does no harm; perhaps it is quite a good thing. He is not old, after all, and he is healthy and vigorous and so soldierly and so dashing. And I could almost say that I was entirely and utterly for him, if only he ... yes, if only he were a little different.”

“In what way, Effi?”

“Yes, in what way. Well, you must not laugh at me. It is something I first pricked up my ears at quite recently, over at the parsonage. We were talking about Innstetten, and all at once old Niemeyer furrowed his brow—but with furrows of respect and admiration—and said: ‘Yes, the Baron! He is a man of character, a man of principles.’”

“And so he is, Effi.”

“Certainly. And I believe Niemeyer even said afterward that he was also a man of firm convictions. And that, I think, is something more still. Oh, and I ... I have none. Look, Mama, there is something in that which torments and frightens me. He is so loving and good to me, and so indulgent, but ... I am afraid of him.”



Chapter Five

The Hohen-Cremmen festivities were over; everyone had departed, including the young couple, who had left on the very evening of the wedding day.

The wedding-eve party had satisfied everyone, especially those taking part in the performance, and Hulda had been the delight of all the young officers, both the Rathenow Hussars and their somewhat more critically disposed comrades from the Alexander Regiment. Yes, everything had gone well and smoothly, almost beyond expectation. Only Bertha and Hertha had sobbed so violently that Jahnke’s Low German verses were as good as lost. But even that had done little harm. Some discerning connoisseurs had even been of the opinion that this was the real thing: faltering, sobbing, and incomprehensibility—under this sign (and especially when the performers were such pretty, red-blond curly heads) the most decisive victories were always won. Cousin Briest had been able to pride himself on a very special triumph in a role of his own composition. He had appeared as a clerk from Demuth’s who, having learned that the young bride intended to travel to Italy immediately after the wedding, wished to deliver a traveling trunk. This trunk naturally proved to be an enormous bonbonnière from Hövel. There had been dancing until three o’clock, during which old Briest, talking himself more and more into a state of supreme champagne exhilaration, had made all manner of remarks about the torch dance still customary at many courts and the curious custom of dancing for the bride’s garter—remarks that showed no sign of ending and, growing more and more extreme, finally went so far that they absolutely had to be stopped. “Pull yourself together, Briest,” his wife had whispered to him in a rather serious tone; “you are not standing here to make double entendres, but to do the honors of the house. We are holding a wedding, not a hunting party.” To which Briest had replied that he saw no such great difference between the two; besides, he was happy.

The wedding day itself had also gone well. Niemeyer had spoken superbly, and one of the old gentlemen from Berlin, who more or less belonged to court society, had remarked on the way back from the church to the wedding house that it was indeed remarkable how richly talents were sown in a state such as ours. “I see in that a triumph of our schools, and perhaps even more of our philosophy. When I consider that this Niemeyer, an old village pastor who at first looked like an almshouse inmate ... yes, my friend, tell me yourself, did he not speak like a court preacher? That tact and that art of antithesis, exactly like Kögel, and in feeling superior to him. Kögel is too cold. To be sure, a man in his position must be cold. What is it that causes one to founder in life, after all? Always warmth alone.” The dignitary to whom these words had been addressed—still unmarried, but perhaps for that very reason involved in a “liaison” for the fourth time—naturally agreed. “Only too true, my dear friend,” he said. “Too much warmth! ... quite superb ... By the way, I must tell you a story later.”
